title: ESPN’s Seth Wickersham Talks Sean Payton, Seahawks’ Sale & More with Rich Eisen | Full Interview
text: Ladies and gentlemen, Seth Wickersham is here on the Rich Eisen Show fresh off of Sean Payton's second chance inside the Denver Broncos Super Bowl posted last week and I you know and I I definitely have a few things flagged but first things first describe to everybody who may not have read this the access that that Sean gave you Seth. >> Yeah, you know, it kind of I would periodically you know, spend a couple days here and there with the Broncos during the season and you know, sometimes I would leave it like two in the morning after their game planning sessions and the idea kind of came up organically where I was like I would I don't to my knowledge. I don't think anybody's ever really witnessed the playoffs from the inside in an unauthorized you know, written type of story where you know, you're there for 14 and 16-hour days and the assignment ends when their season ends whether it's in the first round of the Super Bowl. So that was the idea and Sean signed up for it right away and you know, sure enough a week before you know, the Broncos played the Bills in the playoffs. I was out in Denver and at the facility you know, for some pretty long days mirroring Sean's hours for the most part to try to bring fans as close to the flame as possible about what it takes to try to win at the very very very highest levels of the NFL. >> And what did you glean basically that you put some real great nuggets in there. So before we get to the gleaning here first one that has nothing to do with the playoffs at [laughter] all. I got to hit you on this one. It was the first thing that I jumped off the page when I read it more than anything else. >> Mhm. >> Bill Belichick that that being brought on by Sean Payton to coach the Broncos as for as long as it took to get the requisite number of wins to pass Don Shula. When did he come up with this idea? Was it just right after Bill uh and the Patriots parted ways, Seth? Walk me through the the timeline on this here. >> Yeah, so Sean has a lot of respect for Bill, and they obviously, you know, I think that they they have something in common that they both have the mutual trauma of having, you know, worked under Bill Parcells. And when, you know, Sean was just offended that the league, no team hired Bill Belichick after he and the Patriots split in 2024. And so, his idea, and it was more than like a fleeting thought, but it was less than a full-scale proposal, was, you know, how could he bring him onto the Broncos? And how could he make it appealing to Bill? And one of the things that he thought would be good for Billy and good for the league and possibly good for the Broncos is to bring him on as head coach. So, Sean would temporarily relinquish his throne, become, you know, senior or uh you know, assistant head coach in charge of the offense. And, you know, Bill would coach the Broncos as the head coach, um as many seasons as it took to get him the record. Now, at the end of the day, it was an impossible idea. It was a fanciful idea, but it was something that he, you know, Sean has Something I learned about Sean doing this story is he has astounding creative energy. He thinks of kind of fun, kind of crazy ideas all the time. It just is something that kind of comes naturally to him, and this was one of those things that popped into his head and kind of was something that he he chewed on for a little bit. >> And it went nowhere at the end of the day? >> It went nowhere. I mean, at the end of the day it went nowhere. And um, you know, it was going to be all but impossible to try to enact. But, and who knows if Bill would even wanted to have done it. But, it was something that he did out of he something that he thought of out of respect for Belichick. >> Okay. And now let's get to some of the nuggets for the uh playoffs that you picked up on. Can you tell me about this play called baby shower? Seth. Please. >> Well, that was a play call that they had in the previous years playoffs. So, speaking of respect. So, I mean, Sean Payton has so much respect for Josh Allen and he studies great players in the off season in the chance that they'll play that they might face in the playoffs like how will he strategize for them. And one of the things that he had for Josh Allen is that like this guy is so good and he's so automatic in late game situations that we're not giving him the ball. If they if it's a close game and it's fourth down, we're going to fake a punt. And when they went into the playoffs 2 years ago at Buffalo, he had two fake punts in the game plan and one of them he ran early and it was called baby shower and it was targeting a Bills player whose family had given birth to their first child earlier that week. He knew or just kind of suspected that that guy's head wasn't going to be in the game. And so they came up with this fake punt where the punter throws to Marvin Mims outside. They ran it and it was successful, but yeah, he called it baby shower. That gives you a sense of just how >> amazing. >> diabolical these guys can be. >> And that was the first of the two playoff games that Sean Payton's Broncos have taken on the Bills. That one didn't go well for him and the team. This past one they did win. And so I bring that up to see how his preps for Josh Allen this time around went and anything you gleaned on that front. >> Well, he had another fake punt and it was called Rutgers special. He basically adapted it from a punt that the Raiders ran against the Lions in 2019. He watched all 71 fake punts from, you know, I want to say the past 8 years to try to look for ideas to try to tailor to his own team. In the entire week, he was like, "I'm calling this if it gets close. We're not giving the ball back to Josh Allen." And again, it wasn't out of, you know, worry for their defense. It's just respect for Josh and how good he is. So, they played the Bills. They beat the Bills in overtime. And after that game, we're sitting in his stadium office, and he's kind of just taking in the win. I mean, it had been a long time since he had won a playoff game, and he knew that in a couple days everyone was going to forget about this game. So, he was just kind of tasting the air. And I said, you know, it took almost everything you guys planned for, all of those 2:00 a.m. sessions. And I was like, "You still have Rucker special. You can use it next week if you want." So, I said something like that. And he was like, "No, we we called it." And I [clears throat] was like, "When? Did I go to the bathroom? Like, did I miss this somehow?" And um He says, "No, we called it in overtime." And I'm going, "Wait a second. It was fourth and 11 in overtime, right?" And he grabs my notebook, and he goes, "No, we had the perfect It would have worked." And the players waved it off. And he's he's drawing it up on my notebook. And I was just my head was spinning at the fact that he, you know, the guts and the borderline, you know, gutso and maybe even recklessness that it takes to call a fake punt on fourth and 11 in overtime of a playoff game where the Bills would almost be in field goal range. Um he thought that they had the look, and it was Tyler Badie who called it off. And a little note, Tyler Badie recently celebrated a birthday. And in the team meeting where Sean um wished him happy birthday, he mentioned the fake punt and was like, "You know, we would have had it." >> Wow. >> Well, it all did work out at the end in terms of a result. So, um just to go granular here, were you there? There were two massive plays in that game. The, you know, double possession would be one way to put it. Um and then the other one was Bo Nix hurting himself. What What was What was Sean Payton's postgame Can you share? Uh did he Did he share anything about Yeah, so let's take one play at a time. Um >> Well, first he thought Yeah, he thought that the interception should have never gotten that far because he thought that the Bills held in the end zone and the game should have ended on a safety. But, um look, he was thrilled about the play. I I don't think he thought it was lucky or, you know, a particularly controversial call. Big surprise. But, we were in his office and, you know, look, there's few few things for a football team more pure and electric than winning a playoff game. And you could hear the music, guys are screaming, they're congratulating themselves and each other. And then he's explaining Rucker special to me and the head of the Broncos sports performance, um Beau Lowry, comes in. And he always comes in with an injury report. So, he's holding a piece of paper that has the injuries. And he looks a little solemn that I noticed in retrospect. But, Sean kind of He wanted to keep talking about Rucker special. And he finally He finally turns to Beau and he says, "All right, give it to me." And you know, Beau says, "Beau." And Sean was kind of like, "Beau?" As in what? What Beau are we talking about here? "Beau Nix fractured his ankle. He's having surgery on Tuesday. His season is over." And it was like the room stopped. I mean, the music faded. All of a sudden, you couldn't hear anything. And I mean, he is staring at the ground and he goes, "Stidham." You know, Jerry Stidham. He already He already knew. And then it was interesting because you could see his his eyes start to squint a little bit and his brain was was processing it and he was already thinking about how to message this for the team. And he basically was like, "No one's going to give us a chance. Stidham is better than anybody thinks. Um you know, this is going to This is going to be perfect." But, he knew. He knew in that moment that the chances of winning a Super Bowl were over. He might be able to get past the conference championship, but not the Super Bowl. And that's a really mind-warping feeling to have minutes after you win a playoff game. I mean, you know, I don't think that that's happened really in modern NFL history. There was obviously when um Brock Purdy got hurt early in the NFC Championship game, but that was you know, during the game. I mean, it was a it was a really revealing, vulnerable, and honest moment to witness. So, what did you glean overall? Seth. >> I mean, the torment that it takes to try to win at this level. I know we talk about it, but to witness it and to watch Payton and the Broncos spend an hour, sometimes on a single play, sometimes multiple hours over the course of days. And you know, he nearly broke himself that week. I had I was privy to his sleep scores during the week leading up to the Patriots. And I mean, as the week went on, they were horrible. And it got tense at times with the assistant coaches because, you know, it's 1:30 again and they're still going. Sean's a night owl. He gains steam as the night goes on. And you know, those guys are exhausted. And just what it takes to try to win when, you know, the odds aren't really in your favor when you're starting a backup quarterback, was really startling to see. And you know, we had a moment it was Friday night before the Patriots game and it was like between 6:00 and 8:00 p.m. and he was probably the only coach in, you know, working on that game. Not just in the Broncos building, but even in New England where it was, you know, 2 hours later. And he was working on two more red zone plays to be run against zone defense in the red zone. And I mean, you know, he was grinding through tape again and he was tired. And you know, I was kind of wondering like, you know, is he trying to get a feeling that the game plan is done, or is he really trying to find two plays? And you know, he said at the end of the night before he went home, you know, this is therapeutic for me. And of course, one of the pivotal plays in the Patriots game was that fourth and one that he called, and the Patriots surprised him by running that exact defense that he was preparing for that night. And of course, the Broncos didn't get those are the types of decisions that you live with as a coach, and I think they get heavier and heavier and heavier as you get older, and as you, you know, kind of accumulate scars. >> Is this why he's given up the play calling? To to to Davis Webb, the offensive coordinator in Denver. I'll be honest with you, man. You know, I've known Sean for a long time. >> [clears throat] >> And the idea that he's going to give this up, I was stunned. You know, I was stunned in the execution of it, like Um, I'm wondering how that's going to work this fall, to be honest with you. >> It's so it's so central to his identity. You know, he refers to himself as a play caller as much as he does as a head coach. And you know, but I think there was moments during the season, and I witnessed them and we talked about it, where the insecurity of calling plays was starting to creep in a little bit. And you know, one point he says, it was a lot it's a lot harder to call plays at age 62 than age 42. And I was stunned that he said that, cuz I was like, you know, you're just accumulating experience and knowledge and you know, but I think it's a little bit like when you get a little older, maybe you don't like to drive um, at night in the rain. At least how he put it. And so, you know, I think that it's going to be an interesting transition to Davis Webb. I think that there's going to be moments where Sean overrules him. There's going to be moments where he wants to overrule him and doesn't. There's going to be moments where Davis calls a bad play and Sean takes responsibility for it. But again, you know, going back to that fourth and one against the Patriots, if Davis Webb were calling the plays, might of that sequence ended up differently because Sean initially was going to try to draw them offsides and then he wanted to call a running play and then he called timeout and switched to a passing play. It was like all these things going on in his head and all of these voices in his ear during a critical moment and maybe the operation would have been a little bit cleaner if he's just in charge of the decision with a little bit of input on the play, but Davis is the one making the play. I You know, I don't know. That's me second-guessing and it's not something that I discussed with Sean, but I think that it'll be interesting to see how the Broncos operate this year because again, Sean's a night owl. He likes to stay until 1:30, 2:00 in the morning and I think Davis Webb is going to be the one running those meetings now and so it'll be interesting to see if they're more kind of on a more traditional coach schedule where they start earlier in the morning and leave earlier at night. I'll be honest with you, man, as well. hearing what you said there, I mean, here's a guy who we know um when he when I think he does go into the Hall of Fame um at one point, we will be talking about the onside kick in the Super Bowl that he calls to start the second half. You just brought up the fact that he called a fake punt in a playoff game deep into a playoff game on a fourth and 11. And you just said the word insecure for Sean Payton. I've never heard that word associated with him ever. At any point >> Yeah. >> Seth. >> Well, he's human, you know? And you know, there's there's a little bit of doubt that I think creeps in and I think that um you know, his his creativity and his work ethic is staggering and I detail all of these glimpses about the ways that he entertains the team and tries to prepare them and uses creative methods, whether it's getting players oxygen tanks because he's going to call a lot of no huddle against the Bills in the playoffs and try to use the mile high altitude against the Bills and weaponize it. There's all these interesting things and that stuff just comes to him easily. He's great with the team and I think that um you know the play calling aspect, I'm not saying he's done as a play caller for the rest of his career, but I think that right now he made the decision that for the 2026 Broncos, it's best for that team for Davis Webb to be really a traditional offensive coordinator and have the responsibility to call plays and that authority the same authority that Sean Payton enjoyed when he was under Bill Parcells and he would show Bill Parcells the call sheet the day before games and Parcells would would point at certain play calls and say, "What? Are you trying to make a name for yourself right here?" I think that I think he knows that it's Davis's turn for the time being and um you know, Sean will take a step back and focus more of his time I think on managing the game on Sundays and managing the team during the week, but I mean, you know, that's going to be a transition and I I think he'll still be in the weeds on the planning part of things, but Davis will make the call. >> Before I let you go, Seth, you and Adam Schefter broke the news about the sale of the Seattle Seahawks. I give you the floor on what you want to add, what you learned, anything on that front? Seth >> Well, I think that Vinod Khosla is somebody that not a lot of NFL fans, you know, he's not exactly a household name even though in Silicon Valley he's obviously well known and I think that um someone very early in the process said, you know, "This guy's a killer and don't underestimate his chances to get the team." And you know, sure enough as last week came Adam and I started to hear that he was the favorite and I think that you you at the 11th hour it got a little tight with the Celtics group, but Vinod came through and I think it's going to be a fascinating new owner and I think it's almost, you know, you never know how these things go. But I think it's an ideal situation in the sense that, you know, he's coming in, he's buying a team that obviously is very well run at the moment and his son Neil, I think is going to be heavily involved in day-to-day operations on the team and his son interned with the 49ers back in the day. And you know, everybody always says you always say like, well, what makes a good owner? It's easier to say what makes a bad owner and I think that ownership being involved not in the minutia of football, but in how football operations work, I think can be a really good thing and that will be an interesting case study to see over the coming years how it works in Seattle. >> Well, and then just wrapping it all up with Seattle ownership football footsball World Cup Seattle had a great run in the World Cup so far just up the road here Atlanta, Miami, I could keep going on and on Foxborough the finals are going to be in the New York New Jersey Stadium to use the parlance. Anything you could glean on the way ownership is looking at these World Cups, could it potentially mirror the way some players and if not all players and fans are looking at it like, hey man it's beautiful seeing grass in these places including indoors. Is this World Cup going to potentially leave a lasting world on football operations and the way that the turfs are handled at all Seth? >> Man, I think that like in the near term, I think they'll look at like the broadcast presentation and are there ways that we can adapt, ways that you know, elements of the Fox broadcast which have really been great to our game and see if we can make it a little bit better, but I think that in terms of grass, I mean, look, just this morning I I reached out to an owner and to a team president to ask if, you know, they think the World Cup will influence more owners to adopt grass on their fields, and both of them gave a resounding no. So, I think that's where we're at. >> Can you give me again, you might not have gotten the exact reason, but you you you know ownership very well. You and Don Van Natta are all over that together. >> Why? Why? >> Well, I think it always comes down to cost. And I think that, you know, with the league looking to try to open up negotiations to a new CBA, try to get that that 18th game, that I think they see that as a chip. And, you know, so I'm sure that it'll get done in the next CBA because it's something owners will end up acquiescing on and giving to players, but they're not going to give it preemptively ahead of time. Especially since the players have obviously not shown a huge rush into reopening negotiations what, halfway into a 10-year CBA. >> Mhm. Seth, appreciate the time, man. Thank you, sir. You be well. Great stuff. Uh and then one last thing, pop up Let me see this this cover Mike Hoskins. Uh you've got a book coming up this fall based on your your um on your history. >> work. >> The ESPN >> Well, no, yeah, it's a collection. You know, what's kind of funny, it's you know, it's a collection of my best ESPN work. And so, when it kind of came up, the idea of it came up, you know, it's like a greatest hits for writers. So, of course, I'm wondering, do I have any hits? >> Uh >> Much less any greatest hits. >> Okay. >> But um you know, I was able to cobble together some stories. The Broncos story will be in there. And um you know, it's a collection of work that I'm really proud of over 25 years. And um don't worry, in the fall, I'll be bugging you to try to get on your show to to get word out there. >> Be on That Hill: Stories from the Summits of Sport. Um and it's September 15th. And we know it's it's going to be a great series book cuz you call it sport and not sports. Thanks for the time. >> S's in the title. >> Thanks, man. Good to see you. >> Hey, you made it all the way to the end. Thanks for that. Check us out every single day streaming live on Disney Plus and the ESPN app 12:00 to 3:00 Eastern.

title: FOX Sports’ Maurice Edu on the Keys to Who Wins France vs Spain World Cup Semi | The Rich Eisen Show
text: Fox Sports soccer analyst Maurice Edu right here on the program. I'm going to start this off by just giving you a heads-up here. I'm a relative novice having watched as much soccer as I have over the last 3 weeks as as ever. Are there actual caps? Do you get an actual cap for every every everyone? Is there a real cap? Is there a hat anywhere for it, Maurice? >> [laughter] >> Well, two things. One, I'm glad that you've watched the most soccer this summer. You know, that was the goal. That was the hope. In regards to the caps, I did not actually get a cap every time. Some countries actually do give you caps. You know, one of our colleagues, Peter Crouch, he just got He just got awarded a cap and his cap was kind of unique. They have this program now within England where they're doing these honorary caps for all the players who have been capped for the national team. So, he was I don't remember what number, but a thousand and something and he just got presented with his. But, no, I We in the US, we didn't get a cap. >> All right, let me ask you more relevant questions then. Let's start with the semifinals and how you see this playing out. Start with France and Spain if you don't mind, Maurice. for me. >> Yeah, I like this I really like this match-up between France and Spain. France to me has been Coming into the tournament, they were my pick to win the whole thing and I think they've lived up to the billing. They've been the best team in the attacking phase of the game. They've gotten better defensively. In the group stage, they conceded two goals, but in the knockout rounds, they've yet to concede. So, I look at this team as being the most deep, the most complete, and I would say the most star-studded. Kylian Mbappé, the man you see him there on your screen, just been absolutely elite. title: 2026 Wimbledon: SINNER GOES BACK-TO-BACK As Wimbledon Champion 🏆🎾
text: Welcome to the Wimbledon recap presented by Simply Lemonade. We just had an incredible men's final. I am your host Harry Lyle's Jr. And joining me today are going to be Bill Connelly and Chris Eubanks who is live from London. Gentlemen, excited to have you join me. We just had it like I said an incredible men's final between Yannick Sinner and Alexander Zverev. Four sets to one in Sinner's favor 6-7 7-6 6-3 6-4. Chris, you're on site. What are your initial reactions to what we just saw? >> Yeah, I mean we obviously saw a champion defend his crown but with not without a sturdy test from Alexander Zverev. This was a match-up that I think a lot of people kind of wrote away Alexander Zverev because of how their previous match-ups have been. So far this year Sinner has dominated Zverev in their match-ups but Zverev has made some changes. He won Roland Garros just over a month ago. He's playing a lot more aggressive and on the grass although it's Zverev's least favorite surface it was the most effective surface in this match-up against Yannick Sinner and I think a lot of people were impressed with the aggression that Zverev brought to the court. Really caused Sinner a little bit of issues throughout the course of that match but in the end it was the world number one who just proved a little bit too good in the decisive moments but overall an incredible tournament. Love to see Yannick Sinner back on top playing well and looking forward to seeing how both players progress as they move toward the US hard court swing. >> Yes, Zverev won 81% of his service points in the first set and that was probably that seemed maybe unsustainable at the time but it really was with how Sinner's been serving in this whole tournament most of the year really. Zverev was just going to have to go for his serve in a major major way and he he kept up for a couple sets and then just the the cracks showed in those third and fourth sets just a little bit. >> And if you're watching at home and you missed it let's go ahead and roll the highlight and show you how Yannick Sinner came away with this victory here. Taking him on obviously in the men's final starting off in the second set here. We roll the tape. Um with Center trailing one set to nothing. As we get you see Center there. You love the all white with Wimbledon. Like I said, second set Center trailing one set to nothing. Zverev hits it out on the set point of the tiebreaker set. Evening the match at one set a piece heading into the third. >> [music] >> Rallying back and forth here. The fall. This felt like such a big moment in this match. Coming back here Center the first break of the match. You see Zverev throwing the racket later in the set. Center dialing up 127 miles of straight heat [music] taking a two sets to one lead in the match. Fourth set here leading five games to four and Center beats Zverev with the forehand. His second straight Wimbledon title. And his fifth career Grand Slam. You see the numbers here. It was a pretty even match there. Aces the winners obviously there in Center's favor. The unforced errors though that number definitely sticking out 45 to 25 in favor of Yianni Center in this match again. Felt like we were just going to go back and forth here. It was neck and neck throughout the first couple of sets. Chris what stood out to you the most in those first two sets which felt like perfect tennis by both guys. >> No, very much so. And if for me it kind of we knew what Yianni Center was going to be able to do. We knew he had been serving incredibly well throughout this entire tournament really throughout this entire year. But especially here at Wimbledon he had been so dominant on serve. So we kind of expected that. We expected Alexander Zverev to also be really dominant on his serve. It was going to be a matter about if any guy would be able to seize a break point opportunity. Obviously the first two sets went to tiebreakers. So neither guy able to get the break, but I think the thing that surprised me the most just had to be how committed Alexander Zverev was. We've seen numerous instances in pressure moments where he will get a little bit passive. That was not the case, but because Yanni Sinner is just so confident in his game style, he knows how to play aggressive. He was able to do it over a longer bit of time than Alexander Zverev, but it was a really welcome sight to see from the German to be able to kind of raise that level. But, overall, Yanni Sinner has just proven a bit too good. >> Yeah, there was kind of a warning sign. I was talking about serve percentages there. The warning sign in the second set was as Zverev started losing his second serve a lot more. He was still landing the first, and as long as he did that, he was able to keep up and keep holding, but it really started to wobble in the third set. He only won two of seven second serve points. It really did It did seem to be And again, this is all just the fact that Sinner is pretty much unbreakable right now. Zverev had to be perfect the entire time, and he just couldn't quite keep it up long enough, no matter how no matter how aggressive he was and how assertive he was at different times. >> And look, it was fantastic tennis. I mean, we saw just big serve after big serve after big serve. I know, Chris, though, what was the turning point of the match for you because it felt like for a minute there we were getting ready to go five sets and five tiebreakers. Obviously, that would never happen probably, but it certainly felt like it for a moment. What was the turning point of the match for you? >> Yeah, for me, it it was just a slight drop in the level of Alexander Zverev, and Yanni Sinner kept adjusting his return position and, you know, coming from experience when you're a server, you like to get a rhythm in where your returner is going to stand. Now, when they're constantly moving up and back and left and right, it just gives you a little bit more to think about, and I think that constant pressure throughout the course of the match, combined with Zverev understanding how aggressive Sinner wants to be, and if he has any bit of a let up, Sinner will seize that opportunity. I think just the compound pressure of having to play out of his comfort zone for an extended period of time just gave Sinner a little bit of a glimpse, a little bit of an opening. And once he got that opening, he was finally able to get that initial break in the third set, you kind of felt the tide [music] turning, and you felt like Sinner was going to be able to continue to capitalize, and he would get another break opportunity. So, one slight dip from Alexander Zverev, that's all it took. So, I think this is a step in the right direction for Zverev. I think he will build on this momentum and he's certainly going to be dangerous when we start to get into the North American hard court swing. >> Yeah, he seemed freed. There's no question about that. You know, going from never making a Wimbledon quarterfinal to dropping two sets on the way to the final. How will you remember this Wimbledon final? >> Uh I think that's a great question. I think I'll remember it as an kind of almost a rebirth of Alexander Zverev. Um but I think this is just going to be a step in the right direction and it gets Yiannis Sinner back hoisting a Grand Slam trophy which he hadn't done since Wimbledon last year. So, I think two things both finalists I think are going to build on this momentum. Look for Sinner to be obviously extremely dangerous in the North American hard court swing and will be a threat to win the US Open again, Uh but I think I'll be following the two finalists in Zverev and Sinner as we move toward the rest of the year as almost a bit of a coming out party for different reasons. Zverev to kind of establish himself as more of an aggressive player and Sinner as re-establishing himself at the top of the game lifting up the biggest trophies the game has to offer. >> Chris Eubanks, we appreciate your time, my friend.
